newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England to reform money market operations.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England to reform money market operations.

text.p: The Bank of England on Tuesday announced changes in the way it uses daily money market operations to control interest rates and said the moves were consistent with preparations for a single European currency.

The central bank said it would start using gilt repos -- sale and repurchase agreements in which government bonds are used as collateral for loans -- alongside existing instruments in its daily operations from March 3.

It will also allow a much wider range of banks, building societies and securities firms to trade with it in its market operations instead of just the six venerable "discount houses" with which it has dealt until now.
"That process should help to enhance the efficiency and competitiveness of the sterling money market in London," executive director Ian Plenderleith told a news conference.

In a detailed, technical report entitled "Reform of the Bank of England's operations in the sterling money markets," the bank said the changes were consistent with preparations for a single European currency.
"The changes to be implemented from March 3 are consistent with the direction and spirit of the preparatory work for monetary union published by the European Monetary Institute in January," it said.
The Institute is the forerunner of a future European central bank which will set monetary policy in European Union countries which join a single currency, scheduled to start in 1999.

"The plans being drawn up for monetary operations by the future European Central Bank are relevant to any further development of the Bank's operations, whether or not the United Kingdom participates in monetary union."
Britain's Conservative government negotiated an "opt-out" from the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union (EMU).
But the Bank of England is playing a full part in preparing for EMU in an effort to protect Britain's interests, whether the country is in or out.
Plenderleith said the changes were not specifically intended to be compatible with EMU but were part of an international trend in countries such as the United States, Canada and Japan.

"They are all tending to converge on the same model -- relatively frequent operations in order to be able to conduct fine-tuning when necessary, using prime, liquid open-market instruments," he told Reuters Financial Television.
The bank said the changes related to the mechanics of its daily operations and did not alter its basic approach to implementing monetary policy.
"It remains the objective of the Bank's money market operations to steer short-term interest rates to the levels required to implement monetary policy," it added.

British monetary policy is set by Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke, who takes advice from Bank of England Governor Eddie George at monthly meetings. The two men, who hold their next meeting on Wednesday, have been at odds over policy in recent months.
George, who fears inflation pressures are building up, has been urging Clarke to raise official interest rates from the present 6.0 percent.

The Chancellor, anxious to avoid raising rates in the run-up to the looming election as this would mean dearer home loans for millions of Britons, has so far refused, arguing that the economic signals are mixed.
